questions.question: Why does a glass rod rubbed with silk become positive while an ebonite rod rubbed with fur becomes negative?
questions.solution: Rubbing brings two surfaces into intimate contact; electrons transfer from the material that holds them loosely to the one that holds them tightly. Glass loses electrons (→ positive), silk gains; ebonite gains from fur (→ negative). Charge is never created — only transferred, conserving the total.

questions.question: Why does a charged metal sphere lose its charge through a person's hand while a charged plastic rod does not?
questions.solution: In a conductor, outer electrons are free to move — charge placed anywhere redistributes and drains through any contact path (the hand, which is itself a conductor). In an insulator, electrons are bound to their atoms/molecules: charge stays where it was deposited. Mobility of charge carriers is the whole distinction.

questions.question: Describe how to charge a metal sphere negatively by induction using a positively charged rod, without the rod ever touching it.
questions.solution: Bring the positive rod NEAR the sphere: free electrons in the sphere are attracted toward the near side, leaving the far side positive. Ground the FAR side (touch with finger): electrons flow up from the earth to neutralise the far positive charge. Remove the ground first, then the rod — the sphere is left with the excess electrons (negative). The rod's charge is unchanged: induction rearranges, it does not transfer from the rod.

questions.question: Why do we say charge is 'quantised', and why did Millikan's oil-drop experiment confirm it?
questions.solution: Charge exists only in integer multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C — q = ne, no fractions. Millikan balanced oil droplets in an electric field and found every droplet's charge was a whole-number multiple of the same smallest value. Quantisation follows from charge being carried by discrete particles (electrons, protons).

questions.question: An electron and a positron annihilate into two photons (neutral). Where did the charges go?
questions.solution: Total charge was (+e) + (−e) = 0 before and 0 after — charge is CONSERVED even when the charged particles themselves vanish. Conservation applies to the total, not to individual carriers; annihilation creates neutral photons that carry the zero net charge away.

questions.concept: Why charges inside a conductor move
questions.question: Why does excess charge placed on a conductor end up entirely on its outer surface?
questions.solution: Free electrons repel each other and move until no tangential force remains, which is exactly the condition that the field inside the conductor is zero. Gauss's law then requires zero enclosed charge in the bulk, so all net charge must sit on the surface. Electrostatic equilibrium is the reason: charges redistribute until the field inside vanishes.

questions.concept: Why Coulomb's law needs a medium correction
questions.question: Two charges exert less force in water than in air. Why, and what is the physical quantity that captures this?
questions.solution: Water molecules polarise and partly shield the charges, so a smaller net force is felt. This is packaged as the permittivity ε of the medium: F = q₁q₂/(4πεr²), with relative permittivity (dielectric constant) K = ε/ε₀, roughly 80 for water. Coulomb's law is correct; the medium rescales its strength by a factor 1/K.

questions.concept: Why charging by induction needs a ground connection
questions.question: To charge a sphere by induction you bring a charged rod near and momentarily earth the sphere. Why does earthing make a permanent charge possible?
questions.solution: The rod first redistributes the sphere's own electrons (like charges pushed away, opposite attracted). Earthing lets the repelled charge escape to ground, so the sphere is left with a net charge of the SAME sign as the rod. Remove the earth, then the rod, and the imbalance is trapped. Induction transfers charge only through the ground connection; separating the rod first would cancel everything.
